rejected.title: Spelling patterns from other languages
card: English has borrowed words from many languages. Borrowed words often keep the spelling patterns of the language they came from.
French
endings such as -et in ballet and -que in unique. In these words the final letters are not sounded as they usually would be in English.
Greek
many words with ch said as k, such as chorus and chaos. Greek wrote this sound with the letter chi, which came into English, mostly through Latin, as ch.
Knowing where a word came from helps you spell it. A pattern that looks odd in English may be normal in the language it was borrowed from.
rejected.remember: Odd spellings often come from the language a word was borrowed from.

a.q: Why does the word "unique" end in -que?
opts: It kept the spelling it had in French
It was spelt that way by mistake in English
It is a Greek word with a silent ending
It follows the usual English rule for endings
a.why: English borrowed unique from French and kept the French -que ending. It is not a usual English pattern, so it is not an English rule.
a.clue: Think about which language gave English this ending.

b.q: Layla notices that chorus has ch said as k. What is the best explanation for this spelling?
opts: It came from Greek, whose letter chi became ch in English
It came from French, whose letters ch are said as k
It is a spelling mistake that spread through English
It is a modern English word with no borrowed origin
b.why: Chorus came from Greek, which wrote this k sound with the letter chi. English spells chi as ch but keeps the k sound. French is the tempting choice, but French ch is usually said as sh, not k.
b.clue: Which language wrote this sound with the letter chi?
